chunks: From him, from Ibn Ribat, from Mansur, from Bakr ibn Habib, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
The tailor is not held liable (for loss) except for what his hands have caused, and if you suspect him, you make him swear an oath.

key_terms.أَحْلَفْتَهُ: You make him swear an oath
key_terms.الْقَصَّارُ: The tailor (one who cuts and sews cloth)
key_terms.جَنَتْ يَدَاهُ: What his hands have caused/produced (idiom for direct action/negligence)
key_terms.يُضَمَّنُ: To be held liable or responsible for damage/loss

ai.seo_question: What is the legal liability of a tailor or artisan for lost or damaged goods in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) to define the scope of liability in *ijarah* (contract of hire), distinguishing between direct negligence and external factors. The provision for the artisan to clear themselves via an oath (*yamin*) in case of dispute reflects the Shia juristic emphasis on protecting the worker from excessive burden, a principle later expanded by scholars like al-Murtada and al-Muhaqqiq al-Hilli in their discussions on commercial guarantees.
